canberra.title: Man allegedly sexually abused 11 family or friends over nearly 15 years
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged sexual abuse. Prosecutors allege a man spent years normalising sexualised behaviour aroun...
canberra.content:
Tyson Bonfield (centre, unblurred) approaches the ACT Courts for his trial. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged sexual abuse.

Prosecutors allege a man spent years normalising sexualised behaviour around his family and friends before he sexually assaulted or indecently abused 11 of them.

Tyson ‘Ty’ Bonfield, 46, pleaded not guilty to 43 charges when his jury trial began in the ACT Supreme Court this week.

It is alleged that between the late 2000s and late 2010s, he sexually abused four female members of his own family when they were still children or teenagers.

He is also accused of sexually or indecently assaulting seven family friends – being three teenage girls, three women and one man – over the same period.

The alleged abuse was not reported until one of the children went to Mr Bonfield’s partner in 2020 and told her she had been sexually assaulted for the last two years, ACT Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Trent Hickey said in his opening submissions on Tuesday (1 September).

He said when the partner spoke to Mr Bonfield, the latter claimed the girl was “making it up”.

“I’m not lying … You did this,” the girl reportedly told Mr Bonfield over a later phone call.

Mr Hickey said the family went to police before another one of the teenagers came forward with her own allegations.

“So every day, more came out,” the prosecutor said.

He expected jurors would hear Mr Bonfield often walked around his house naked while other people were over and would touch or comment on women’s bodies.

It was expected a family member would tell the jury he was always being inappropriate, with some people remarking, “That’s just Ty being Ty”.

Mr Hickey alleged Mr Bonfield had gradually desensitised others to his sexualised behaviour, which normalised an environment for sexual conduct to occur.

Among the allegations against him, the first offence he was alleged to have committed took place after a house party at his home in 2007.

It is alleged the first adult family friend woke up to him kissing her before he tried to orally rape her. She allegedly tried to push him off, but he only stopped when they heard another person making noise in the house.

In 2008, a teenage member of his family was staying over at his place, drinking alcohol. When she became drunk, he allegedly orally raped her, too.

It is alleged that when she confronted him years later, he told her, “I didn’t make you do anything you didn’t want to”.

Tyson Bonfield has pleaded not guilty to all charges in his trial. Photo: Albert McKnight.

Then in 2016, Mr Bonfield allegedly tried to rape another teenage member of his family.

“She was scared of the accused and always had been, because he was violent,” Mr Hickey alleged.

He also allegedly took her to a sex shop when she was still under 18 and bought her a vibrator, then later asked her, “Have you used it?”

The last family member, whose claims led to the family going to police, alleged he had gone into her bedroom and raped her in 2020.

Mr Hickey said Mr Bonfield denied the allegations, so he expected the main issue for the jury in the trial would be whether they were satisfied that the charged conduct occurred.

The first witness in the trial was the second adult family friend. When speaking to police in 2024, she alleged Mr Bonfield groped her at a party and tried to force her to give him oral sex during a drive in his Chrysler 300.

“When I first met him, he came across as a nice person. A bit on the sleazy side,” she said.

“The further along our relationship went as friends … he turned out not to be such a great person.”

The woman alleged he had often acted inappropriately with women by walking around his house naked or touching their bodies.

She claimed his partner had asked him to stop “on thousands of occasions”.

“He felt he was entitled to be able to touch whoever he could,” the woman claimed.

“Ty was very full-on, just all over people. More so women than males.”

The four members of Mr Bonfield’s family named in the charges have provided their consent to the media to name him in reporting. While they were children or teenagers at the time of the alleged offending, they are now all adults.

The trial continues before Chief Justice Lucy McCallum.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on (02) 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on (02) 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on (02) 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

You can also submit an online report about a historical sexual assault allegation for incidents that occurred more than six months ago.

canberra.title: Warmest winter on record sets stage for potentially scorching spring
canberra.snippet: Climate change shifted into high gear this year as the ACT experienced the warmest winter on record, with above-average temperatures set ...
canberra.content:
Spring has sprung in Canberra after a warm winter. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Climate change shifted into high gear this year as the ACT experienced the warmest winter on record, with above-average temperatures set to continue into the spring.

The mean winter maximum of 14.6 degrees Celcius recorded at Canberra Airport was 1.1 degrees above average, while the mean minimum was 1.7 degrees, 0.9 degrees above average.

Bureau of Meteorology climatologist Qian Zhou said winter temperatures were above average right across the ACT, with significantly warmer winter nights.

“I have to say both mean maximum temperature and the mean minimum temperatures are the highest on record across ACT, with the mean minimum temperature very much above average,” she said.

Ms Zhou said several factors were behind the record winter temperatures, including the long-term trend of global warming.

But an above-average subtropical ridge and warmer seas also played a part.

“The above-average subtropical ridge resulted in generally settled conditions and the warmer daytime temperatures,” Ms Zhou said.

“Additionally, warmer than average sea surface temperatures along the southern New South Wales coast and over the Tasman Sea likely limited the overnight cooling.”

Ms Zhou said the subtropical ridge’s intensity in July was the second-highest on record, and in June and August it was also above average in parts of the south and east, resulting in sunny days and warm temperatures.

This also contributed to this winter’s low snowfall, which led to poor skiing conditions in the Alps and forced resorts to close their ski fields early.

Ms Zhou said declining snowfall was a long-term trend.

“The maximum snow cover and the number of snow days have all decreased in Australian alpine regions since the late 1950s,” she said.

While August brought a cold spell, it had rained beforehand, melting whatever snow had accumulated.

Looking to spring, the bureau is forecasting a drier, warmer season with an increased fire risk.

Ms Zhou said rainfall was likely to be below average across the ACT and maximum and minimum temperatures were very likely to be above average with an increased chance of unusually warm days and nights.

She said the El Niño in the Pacific Ocean was likely to be the strongest on record since reliable records began from 1950, but this did not always mean a commensurate impact on Australia’s weather.

Typically, El Niño resulted in reduced rainfall over parts of eastern and southern Australia during winter and spring.

Ms Zhou said global warming had led to a long-term decline in rainfall over southern Australia, along with warmer temperatures during the cool season.

But it looked like a positive Indian Ocean Dipole was forming, which usually also led to less rainfall in central and southern Australia.

Canberra’s warm start to spring will continue for the rest of the week with temperatures in the late teens or 20s, and some rain tipped for Saturday.

On the South Coast, Batemans Bay will bask in a sunny, 27-degree day on Wednesday, with fine days and low to mid-20s maximums for the rest of the week.

canberra.title: Treasury warns Australia risks missing out on global AI boom
canberra.snippet: The take-up of artificial intelligence in Australian businesses is low, with less than 10 per cent of firms reporting a significant adopt...
canberra.content:
Treasury analysis prepared for Treasurer Jim Chalmers suggests Australia could miss out on an economic boom if AI is not more widely adopted. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The take-up of artificial intelligence in Australian businesses is low, with less than 10 per cent of firms reporting a significant adoption of the technology.

This analysis has led Treasury to warn that Australia could miss out on the economic benefits of the AI boom unless wider use of AI is embraced.

The department has given Treasurer Jim Chalmers its detailed analysis of where the nation stands on AI, with advice that businesses should be encouraged to change their attitudes.

About two-thirds of businesses report using some AI, but mostly in a superficial way.

Capital investments, organisational changes and workforce skills were cited as reasons firms have not moved beyond the basic use of AI in their business practices.

Companies involved in finance, insurance, information, telecommunications and professional services have led Australia’s adoption of AI, while health care, education, construction and tourism are proving slower to make the transition.

Australia has 162 operational AI data centres, with another 130 or so on the drawing board.

Treasury’s advice is that job losses have not yet materialised as feared, and the AI boom could pass Australia by without a change in mindset.

It is, however, monitoring international signs for job losses in entry-level positions.

The Treasurer’s reported response is that Australia could make the most of the benefits of AI while also minimising the risks of what he describes as the “biggest economic transformation in our lifetime”.

He said advances in AI were happening so fast, with new milestones being reached in weeks rather than years. Australia had to take advantage of the opportunities presented.

“We can’t just sit around and hope the benefits of AI fall into our lap,” Dr Chalmers said.

“We have to reach out and take them.”

The Federal Government is preparing legislation to regulate the rollout of AI, including how data centres must operate.

Except in Queensland and the Northern Territory, new data centres will have to use renewable energy.

Other conditions will govern how energy and water are used, where the centres are located, how local jobs are maintained, and how the rights of authors and artists are protected.

The Federal Government has been forced into committing to these protective measures in the face of widespread public concerns over AI.

But it aims to go full steam ahead in attracting the massive investment AI data centres promise to bring to Australia.

The Treasury analysis points to an AI-supported long-term annual productivity growth of 1.2 per cent.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) says it believes Australia can seize its share of the AI opportunity, but only if the nation’s economic settings are calibrated correctly.

Chief executive officer Andrew McKellar said the current regulatory and tax settings are not where they need to be to make the most of “this AI moment” in Australia.

“Artificial intelligence is reshaping Australia’s economy. It is changing how businesses deliver services and how Australians access them,” he said.

“AI offers the opportunity to lift Australia’s ailing productivity growth over the next decade, but only if we get the fundamental regulatory environment right.

“Australian business and industry will be able to compete in the AI-era if given a fair go and a level playing field with international competitors.

“Expecting Australian businesses to globally compete on AI while loading them up with excessive tax and regulatory burdens does not compute.

“Australian businesses should not have to engage in this competition with one hand tied behind their backs.”

The ACCI boss said Australian businesses are not only handicapped by one of the highest company tax rates in the developed world, but also by worsening business tax settings.

He said the Federal Budget introduced a “major tax hike” on business investment.

“We also must ensure Australia has policy settings that enable the responsible growth of data centres, not stand in their way,” Mr McKellar said.

“Data centres are critical infrastructure and an essential component of Australia’s future prosperity.

“The policy challenge is not whether data centres should be built, but how they can best be planned, powered and resourced efficiently while maintaining community and investor confidence.”

canberra.title: Medical negligence tops $60 million as abuse and footpath claims add to ACT costs
canberra.snippet: Medical negligence claims cost the ACT more than $60 million in damages, settlements and legal expenses last financial year – more than d...
canberra.content:
The ACT Insurance Authority paid almost $51.9 million in damages and settlements relating to medical negligence in 2025-26. Photo: James Coleman.

Medical negligence claims cost the ACT more than $60 million in damages, settlements and legal expenses last financial year – more than double the bill just two years earlier.

The figure is the largest among a series of legal costs revealed in Budget Estimates questions by independent Member for Kurrajong Thomas Emerson, who says the financial impact of Canberrans taking their own government to court warrants greater scrutiny.

ACT Solicitor-General Peter Garrison revealed the ACT Insurance Authority paid almost $51.9 million in damages and settlements relating to medical negligence in 2025-26, along with another $8.85 million in legal costs.

That compares with $30.1 million in damages and settlements and $9 million in legal costs in 2024-25.

In 2023-24, damages and settlements stood at $21.3 million, with a further $7.3 million spent on legal costs.

Across the three financial years, medical negligence claims alone have therefore cost more than $128 million.

“Nobody’s talking about the budgetary impact of Canberrans suing their own government. These figures show the whole-of-government cost of incompetence is massive,” Mr Emerson said.

The figures come as the ACT Government faces continuing pressure over the Territory’s financial position.

Mr Emerson’s questions followed observations by the Chief Minister and Treasurer regarding the budget, which raised concerns about fiscal sustainability without identifying clear spending cuts or additional revenue.

Mr Emerson argues the government’s legal bill should itself be part of that conversation.

“While not every lawsuit is avoidable, the ACT Government should be closely investigating the impact of its growing legal bill on the Territory’s finances. This is a clear avenue for the government to improve its fiscal sustainability.”

The Estimates answers also reveal dozens of institutional abuse claims have been lodged in recent years.

There were 23 matters opened in 2023-24, 17 in 2024-25 and 46 in 2025-26 – 86 matters across the three years.

Only eight of those matters have so far been settled, with the Territory contributing approximately $3.2 million towards settlements, including claimants’ legal costs and disbursements.

The Territory also incurred about $126,000 in its own disbursements, while legal services provided by the ACT Government Solicitor were funded separately.

The claims include matters involving institutional abuse, which can include child sexual abuse.

The final cost of the remaining cases is not yet known. The government noted that institutional abuse claims involving alleged abuse after 1 July 1998 are generally covered by the ACT Insurance Authority.

Another multimillion-dollar bill is arising from something Canberrans encounter every day – footpaths.

The ACT Government spent $7.18 million maintaining and repairing footpaths in 2025-26.

During the same year, the ACT Insurance Authority spent another $2.77 million on personal injury claims stemming from footpath-related issues.

That means the cost of footpath injury claims was equivalent to almost 39 per cent of what the government spent maintaining and repairing paths.

“How many footpaths could have been repaired with the millions of dollars spent on payouts and legal costs?” Mr Emerson said.

Government figures show new concrete paths typically cost between $280 and $300 per square metre, while asphalt paths can range from $100 to $300 per square metre and crushed aggregate paths from $120 to $220 per square metre. Costs can vary considerably depending on the site and project.

Civil proceedings involving ACT Policing provide another part of the picture, although the government has not disclosed their financial cost.

As of 6 August, the Australian Federal Police was a named respondent in 29 civil proceedings currently before the courts relating to ACT Policing actions.

Of those, 18 – more than 60 per cent – relate to, or include, claims involving the use of force.

The figures do not include proceedings involving ACT Policing employment conditions, administrative law matters or other cases against the AFP.

Mr Emerson also asked how many civil cases ACT Policing had faced during the past five financial years, how many had been settled out of court and the cost of settlements, legal expenses and damages involving use-of-force cases.

Those figures were not provided.

The government said retrieving them would require manually examining numerous physical and electronic AFP files because record-keeping methods had changed over the five years, amounting to an “unreasonable diversion of resources”.

canberra.title: South Coast trekker believed to have died in Nepal floods as partner redirects fundraiser to victims
canberra.snippet: NSW South Coast man Michael Keats is believed to have died in the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods after being caught in the disaster whil...
canberra.content:
Emily Bond and her partner, Michael Keats, who is believed to have died in the Nepal floods. Photo: Emily Bond.

NSW South Coast man Michael Keats is believed to have died in the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods after being caught in the disaster while returning from a spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.

The journey had been a long-held dream for Michael, whose partner Emily Boyd described as deeply devoted to his spiritual practice.

He had been due to arrive home when his group was caught in the catastrophic flooding near an immigration centre on the Nepal-Tibet border.

Before his death was confirmed, Emily described waking to messages from Michael’s family and a volunteer from the Isha Foundation telling her about the disaster.

With communications to the disaster-hit region cut, the family initially had no way of knowing what had happened to him.

“We are all shocked and devastated. I feel sick to the stomach, heavy in the heart and my mind is racing,” Emily said in a social media post.

Back home on the NSW South Coast, his friends were also desperately hoping for good news. Four days before news of his death emerged, friend Jemie Lepre called on the local community to gather at Mollymook for a prayer circle for Michael.

“We’ve got this prayer group to pray, to call in Michael Keats, to call him back home safe and sound,” he said.

With little else they could do from thousands of kilometres away, friends were asked to bring instruments, candles and items for an altar and join their intentions for Michael’s safe return.

“Drum up this energy to create a miracle because we will need a miracle to ensure his safety,” Mr Lepre said.

That miracle did not come.

Emily described the sudden loss of a man who had been central not only to her life, but to their family and household.

“We are trying to navigate the shock and grief of losing someone we love deeply, while also suddenly having to face life without the person who was such an important part of our family and our household,” she said.

She later spoke about the future they had imagined together – including Michael’s hope of having a baby and her son’s wish for a brother or sister.

“Mike really wanted to have a baby, Jai really wanted to have a brother or a sister, and all of the different places that we wanted to visit and all of the different things that we wanted to do,” she said.

Michael Keats described himself as a spiritual man. Photo: Instagram.

Emily and Jai were subsequently invited to travel to India to take part in a spiritual ritual connected with Sadhguru to honour Michael on September 3.

For Emily, the invitation initially carried particular significance because of Michael’s own spiritual beliefs and the journey he had been making when he died. Michael, who had completed a master’s of teaching, once described himself as a “teacher, a guide, a nature lover, and a mystic at heart”.

Emily launched a GoFundMe campaign to help meet the cost of travelling to India and to support the family as they dealt with the immediate financial impact of his death.

But with the ceremony only days away, she found herself racing to arrange passports, visas and flights while trying to process her partner’s death.

“I’m just scrambling trying to get passports updated and visa applications and looking at flights and whatnot,” she said in an emotional social media post.

“In and amongst trying to just navigate grief and messages from hundreds of people around the world and journalists and media … honestly it’s been the craziest time of my life.”

A day later, she told supporters the trip would not be possible. After spending hours trying to organise the necessary documents, Emily said there was not enough time to update Jai’s passport and secure visas before they would have needed to leave.

With the India trip abandoned, Emily said a large portion of the money donated through the fundraiser would instead go to people affected by the Nepal floods.

Some would also help Michael’s sisters, two of whom were travelling overseas, while the remainder would help Emily cover everyday expenses and time away from work as she grieves.

“I know the whole community is suffering as well,” she said.

“I will be donating a large portion of the money to the people affected by the floods in Nepal.”

Emily said she planned to step away from social media and spend time alone in nature as she tried to process what had happened.

As of 1 September, her fundraiser had raised more than $30,000.

The tragedy comes as the Australian Government ramps up its consular and humanitarian response to the disaster, with about 43 Australians reported missing.

Officials are working to establish their welfare, while additional personnel have been deployed to Kathmandu. A Crisis Response Team member and a regional consular officer are already on the ground, with further support being prepared.

The government is also sending an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists through the Australia Assists program to support Australian personnel already in the region. The team has expertise in humanitarian assessment, logistics, communications and planning.

Australia has announced $5 million in humanitarian assistance for communities affected by the floods on both sides of the Nepal-China border.

The package includes $2 million for the World Food Programme, which has already dispatched food rations and provided logistics support for Nepal’s emergency response.

Another $2 million will go to Australian NGOs through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership to provide emergency shelter, hygiene kits, blankets, medical and psychosocial support.

The remaining $1 million will go to the Emergency Action Alliance to support locally led recovery and rehabilitation.

The floods have swept away villages, damaged critical infrastructure and displaced thousands of people. Roads and bridges have also been destroyed, leaving communities isolated and making search, rescue and recovery efforts more difficult. More than 900 people have already been confirmed dead.

australia.title: Australians missing in the Nepal floods: what we know so far
australia.snippet: There are 42 Australians among the thousands of people missing as rescue efforts continue after deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet bo...
australia.content:
The number of Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet flash flooding disaster fell from 43 to 42 on Tuesday, with the announcement that one of the unaccounted for people had made contact from Tibet.

Pilgrims trekking to a holy site in Tibet make up the majority of Australians who have been reported missing after deadly flash floods and landslides tore through valleys on the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday last week. Most were travelling with Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Kailash Journeys and the Isha Foundation.

The announcement that a second Australian had been found alive on Tuesday comes after Sydney woman Cara Severino, 25, was safely located last week.

Due to privacy obligations, Dfat has not provided further details about the second Australian to be found alive.

Across Nepal and Tibet, thousands of people have been reported missing and Nepali and Chinese authorities have confirmed hundreds have died.

Here’s what we know about the Australians who remain missing. This article will be updated as more information becomes available.

Venkatraman Balakrishnan and Chitra Venkatraman

New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were among 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash on a spiritual trip with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group.

Their son, Akash Venkatraman, said his parents had planned to leave their riverside accommodation in Syabrubesi before it was devastated by flood waters.

Muralitharan family

Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, Chandresekaran Muralitharan, 47 and their children Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were also taking part in the Himalayan Glacier Adventures spiritual tour to Mount Kailash when the flood hit.

The parents and two children had been training together for the long walk, Shylaja’s younger sister Vaishnavi said.

She lost contact with the family shortly after their breakfast on the morning of the flood.

Iyer family

Sreedharan Iyer, 52, and Lakshmi Iyer, 50, and their adult sons Rishab Iyer, 23, and Rudhra Iyer, 20, were taking part in the spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash with Himalayan Glacier Adventures.

The Iyer brothers are medical students at the University of Newcastle and members of the West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook Cricket Club in Sydney’s north-west.

Karan Bhardwaj, Arpan Mithalal Kothari and Bhavin Raval

Karan Bhardwaj, Arpan Mithalal Kothari and Bhavin Raval were travelling together on a Kailash Journey tour of the region. Bhardwaj’s family says the three men have known each other since 2009, when they met at university.

Raval’s wife, Bhavinkumar Raval, has told the ABC she believes her husband is still alive and is making plans to travel to Nepal.

Bhardwaj is a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian Air Force.

Bhardwaj’s family member Jen said: “Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law. He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”

Narayan Panthi

Narayan Panthi, from Brisbane, has been listed by Nepali police as travelling with operator Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel. It is understood Panthi had been carrying out independent volunteer charity work in Kathmandu earlier in the week before travelling towards the border region.

Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, told Guardian Australia his family were devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.

“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”

Bhusal said Panthi had been “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”.

Bharat Mangwani

Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.

He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu.

“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.

Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has flown to Nepal to look for him.

Sumi Adhikari

Sumi Adhikari, 41, was at the Gyirong Port crossing with the Isha Foundation group when the flood hit.

Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal seeking information about her whereabouts.

“We still have no clear or official information about Sumi or the other members of her group,” Pandey said on Saturday morning.

Renee Spry

A Sunshine Coast disability support worker, Renee Spry has been described as a “deeply spiritual” person who travelled to Nepal on a pilgrimage.

“She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation. Her priority was always other people,” her sister Clair Spry said.

“Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.”

Clair Spry has set up a GoFundMe so her family can travel to Nepal to look for signs of Renee.

Suhasini Kandimalla

A mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, Suhasini Kandimalla was hiking with another Springfield local, according to her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla.

While she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned.

“I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini said of the Nepal trip.

“But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.”

Reshma Patel

Newcastle woman Reshma Patel, 46, was in the Isha Foundation group. She didn’t know Sumi Adhikari beforehand, but the pair had become friends on the pilgrimage, Patel’s family friend Chin Valsan says.

“They were talking to each other, and they were supposed to come back on the same flight on Thursday,” he says.

He describes Patel, who has two children aged 10 and 14 and works casually for Canterbury-Bankstown council, as “full of life” and a “kind soul” who loves her family and friends.

Kanagamah Sundrasan

The mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, was part of the Kailash Journey trek to Mount Kailash.

Her daughter, Swaatika Kanniah, said her mother had been excited about the hike.

“It was a pilgrimage, she really wanted to go and have that experience.”

A photograph of her on the trip shows her smiling with five other members of the tour; all are now missing.

“I feel like everyone is trying their best, but yes we don’t know much about what’s going on,” Kanniah said of the recovery efforts.

Michael Keats

The family of 37-year-old Michael Keats, from Mollymook in NSW, said on social media that he had died.

Keats’s partner, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram on Sunday that he had been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which had been his “dream for many years”.

“Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said.

“There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted [than] to know God, and to merge with the divine.

“He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.”

On Tuesday, the foreign minister, Penny Wong, said the Australian government “has not yet received official confirmation of Mr Keats’ passing. He does remain unaccounted for in terms of the information we have. But … we respect the rights of the families to make the statements they have”.

“Our thoughts go out to his family and to every Australian family who is hoping that the many who are missing can be located,” she said.

Luke Costanzo

Luke Costanzo, 30, from Perth remains missing, his family has confirmed.

He was on a pilgrimage trek with the Isha foundation, and the group was last in contact at the Gyirong port border crossing as they were making their way back to Kathmandu on the final day of their journey, the family said in a statement.

“Luke is an extremely strong, compassionate, disciplined and spiritual person. Once he makes a decision he commits to it fully and he was so excited to be visiting Mount Kailash on a pilgrimage trek with the Isha Foundation,” the family said.

“We truly appreciate all the love and support from friends and family that we’ve received and ask everyone to keep Luke, and all those affected, in your thoughts and prayers.”

The family has asked people who wish to help to donate “to aid the wonderful people on the ground who continue with rescue efforts”.

australia.title: Sydney records warmest winter on record as Melbourne equals previous hottest temperatures
australia.snippet: New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania just experienced their warmest-ever winters – and BoM says above-average temperatures expected to ...
australia.content:
Australia’s two biggest cities had their hottest and equal hottest winters on record, with three eastern states also breaking temperature records.

The Bureau of Meteorology’s (BoM) spring outlook shows above average daytime and night-time temperatures are expected to continue for much of the country, with an increased chance of unusually high maximums.

Dr Simon Grainger, a senior climatologist at the bureau, said Sydney had its warmest winter on record, with the mean temperature of 15.3C at Observatory Hill breaking the previous record of 15.0C set in 2013. Average maximum and minimum temperatures at the same site were also the warmest on record.

Melbourne equalled its 2005 record for winter mean temperature of 12.2C, while Canberra recorded its warmest winter maximum, with an average maximum temperature of 14.7C.

New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania had their warmest winters on record, and all other states and territories except the Northern Territory were in their top 10 warmest winters on record since 1910.

Australia’s mean temperature was 1.45C above the 1961–1990 average for winter, the equal third-highest on record since national observations began in 1910.

Grainger said much of the south-east’s experience was driven by “relatively warm nights and a lot fewer cold nights”, with several factors at play.

“The local weather patterns certainly assisted. For large parts of this winter we had high pressure systems sitting in the Tasman sea,” he said.

“That allowed a lot of warmer air to come down from the tropics over eastern Australia – places like Sydney, Canberra, Melbourne – with fewer outbreaks of cold air getting in.”

Grainger said the developing strong El Niño had also set up weather patterns that tended to be favourable for high daytime temperatures across southeastern Australia.

“Finally of course, all of this is occurring against the background of a globally warmer climate,” he said.

“Daily [global] land temperatures and daily ocean temperatures during August have been close to or above the historical records that were set only in 2024.”

Australia’s national annual average temperature is about 1.5C higher than in 1910, according to the BoM, and the climate crisis, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, has increased the frequency and severity of extreme weather events.

The record-breaking winter data was released as federal resources minister Madeleine King and Northern Territory chief minister Lia Finocchiaro celebrated turning on the tap that will feed the first fracked gas from the Beetaloo Basin into the territory’s power grid.

It follows a horror northern hemisphere summer of record-breaking heatwaves, drought and wildfires in Europe and North America, and intense rain and typhoons in Asia.

The national average rainfall for winter was 8% above the 1961–1990 average, driven by high rainfall in southern inland Australia. Grainger said parts of inland NSW, Victoria, South Australia and parts of the Northern Territory had above average rainfall, with parts of far-western NSW near the SA border experiencing their wettest winter on record.

SA recorded its sixth wettest winter on record. In contrast, rainfall was below average in parts of the east coast and south-western Australia.

The BoM’s long-range forecast shows below average rainfall is expected to continue through parts of southern and eastern Australia through spring, while above average rainfall is expected in large parts of the west from October.

Grainger said a continuation of above average daytime and night-time temperatures was likely for much of the country “and with that there’s [a] chance of unusually high maximum and minimum temperatures”.

He said the BoM’s models showed the El Niño in the Pacific Ocean would continue to strengthen through spring, likely peaking in late spring or in summer.

Prof Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick, a climate scientist from the Australian National University, said while some people might enjoy the idea of a warmer winter, it had negative consequences for the environment.

“We need to consider what’s happening to our natural ecosystems,” she said.

“A lot of our ecosystems need cooler temperatures, a lot of our animals are used to it, and if we start taking that out of the picture, then things aren’t looking so healthy.”

She pointed to the recent snow season, where low falls had also affected the tourism industry, with resorts in Victoria and NSW forced to close early.

“Snowfall in Australia is pretty rare, and just notching the temperature up to a couple of degrees during winter basically puts us above freezing point most of the time,” she said.

australia.title: Footage of police officer boasting about punching Sydney anti-Herzog protester raises questions about conduct
australia.snippet: Male police officer caught on camera during 9 February protest against visit of Israeli president Isaac Herzog Get our breaking news emai...
australia.content:
Video footage has emerged capturing a New South Wales police officer boasting about “punching” a protester in the head “when he was down”, before the protester was charged with assaulting police.

Police body-worn camera footage, which was leaked to a social media account and widely shared over the weekend, reveals a male police officer telling his colleagues during the 9 February protest at Sydney town hall against a visit by the Israeli president, Isaac Herzog: “I fucking pumped that cunt.”

A female officer can be heard replying, “So funny,” before the male officer says: “Then I punched him in the head when he was down.”

Guardian Australia understands the video relates to legal proceedings from a protester who was charged with assaulting police. They were one of three protesters who on Friday had the charges against them dropped.

Police have now withdrawn charges against four of the 30 protesters charged in the wake of the protest. The three protesters who had their charges withdrawn on Friday were scheduled to face a joint hearing alongside 22 others in July 2027.

The premier, Chris Minns, had previously urged the public “to not look at a 10-second clip without the full context” after a number of videos went viral showing police allegedly punching protesters and dragging Muslim worshippers away while they were praying.

The new video of the police bragging about punching the protester is understood to be the first bodycam footage to be widely shared publicly.

In February, the independent police watchdog – the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) – launched Operation Makalu to investigate allegations of police brutality at the protest.

On Tuesday, the NSW Greens MP and spokesperson for justice, Sue Higginson, referred the leaked body-worn camera footage to the watchdog, alleging it was evidence of police misconduct.

“The police misconduct that I personally witnessed on 9 February at town hall was obscene, the impunity was something I have not ever seen before and I have no doubt it was the result of the Minns Labor government suppressing protest with invalidly made laws,” Higginson said in a statement.

“This footage shows the attitude of the police that night and should result in an immediate suspension and investigation of the officers involved.

“The Lecc is already investigating the actions of the police that night, but this evidence warrants immediate action by the NSW police.”

A spokesperson for NSW police said they were aware of the video, but were unable to comment due to the ongoing Lecc investigation.

Guardian Australia approached Minns for comment.

The day after the protest, he said that the police were “put in an impossible situation” after protesters attempted to defy the public assembly restriction declaration (Pard) law, which police enforced during the protest.

In April, the court of appeal found that law unconstitutional, ruling in favour of the Palestine Action Group and Blak Caucus who brought a challenge against it.

Majed Kheir, a lawyer who represented two of the three protesters whose charges were on Friday withdrawn, said: “The withdrawal of a further three cases simply reflects recognition of the reality that these cases were doomed to fail.

“The brutal conduct of police on 9 February plainly went so beyond the pale. All charges should be immediately dropped as a first step to restore some level of confidence in the NSW police force that our law enforcement institution can be accountable and acknowledge their wrongdoing.”

A petition launched in June by the NSW Council for Civil Liberties calling for the charges against all the anti-Herzog protesters to be dropped has almost 3,000 signatures.

australia.title: Albanese has everything to lose engaging in a fight with Hanson, but he may be drawn in anyway | Analysis
australia.snippet: The PM wants to combat One Nation through core Labor values such as education and health, even as his popularity takes a beating Sign up ...
australia.content:
At the height of her 1998 re-election fight, Pauline Hanson was challenged to give her honest assessment of John Howard.

Two years on from her firebrand maiden speech, the One Nation leader was contesting the Queensland seat of Blair when she was bailed up by a group of punters at a country race meeting. The men had been drinking and one demanded to know if Howard was “a prick”.

Hanson told them that the country’s leader had a job to do and she respected his position as the prime minister.

“You have a go at someone if you disagree with their policies or their views,” she counselled. “Don’t denigrate the person just for the fact that you don’t agree with him.”

Nearly 30 years on, with her party soaring in the opinion polls, Hanson is taking a very different approach.

One Nation claims to have raised millions from its “fire the liar” fundraising drive targeting Anthony Albanese, and Hanson cut sick on Sunday after the prime minister gave a speech describing the politics of “hard-right populists” as “dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest”.

Attracting as much media attention as at any point in her career, Hanson posted on social media that Albanese’s comments to the Queensland Labor conference, a day after One Nation’s win in the Secret Harbour byelection in Western Australia, “crossed a line”. She claimed the comments were “how political violence is incited” and referenced the death of British politician Ann Widdecombe in July, an alleged murder being investigated by counter-terrorism police.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s new Politics, really newsletter here

It’s worth remembering Hanson had no sympathy for the then Victorian premier, Jacinta Allan, when she faced misogynist attacks earlier this year. Hanson’s advice was “suck it up, sweetheart”.

It suits the leader of the insurgent minor party to attack Labor, in an attempt to attract headlines and drag Albanese into a slanging match.

She has name-checked the prime minister, the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, and other politicians including Andrew Hastie and Matt Canavan in her feed in recent days.

But engaging in the fight is all downside for Labor.

Albanese has repeatedly called for the temperature of politics to be turned down, and wants to fight One Nation on politics and policy, not personal insults. Albanese did not actually attribute his “dangerous, divisive, and downright dishonest” comments to One Nation specifically – but that fact didn’t matter to Hanson.

Albanese’s long-held view is that driving down One Nation’s support in time for the next election is best achieved through a fight on core Labor values, such as education policy, health, paid parental leave and compulsory superannuation.

Labor sources privately point to Peter Dutton’s standing in January 2025, when polls showed the Coalition competitive in the months before the looming election. Some Liberals thought Dutton was on track to become prime minister, and just five months later he was booted from parliament as Labor romped home with 94 seats.

Albanese’s personal standing could suffer from Hanson’s attacks too.

The latest Newspoll had Albanese’s net approval rating at minus 21, with 38% of voters satisfied with his performance and 59% dissatisfied. In the Resolve poll, just 37% of voters said the prime minister was doing a good or very good job, compared with 53% who said his performance was poor or very poor – for a net score of minus 16 percentage points.

With the election likely more than a year away, Albanese can afford to try to rise above Hanson’s attacks, even if she no longer respects the office of prime minister quite as much as she used to.

world.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
world.snippet: Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks Airlink insists flyby conducted according to regulations A pre-game stunt involving...
world.content:
A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.

Airlink, a sponsor of the South Africa rugby union team, said the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft flying at 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over a stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But the flyby last weekend was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa, said. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said yesteron Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.Airlink said flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

world.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
world.snippet: Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination A UN committee has said countries...
world.content:
A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.

The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.

“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.

At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.

Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.

Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.

Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

world.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration Spain’s prime minister,...
world.content:
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.

“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday. “Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”

Sánchez said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.

The accusation drew a furious response from Israel. The country’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, called it a “brazen lie”, adding: “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not distract from Sánchez’s disgraceful failure to manage his country’s affairs.”

The ⁠Kremlin rejected allegations ⁠that ​Russia was connected to ⁠the Ceuta migration crisis, the ⁠RBC daily ​reported ‌on ‌Monday.

Sánchez repeated his assertion that the influx was due to the activities of “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.

Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, at least 5,000 people, including 1,200 minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta. Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.

Sánchez said there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.

Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.

world.title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city
world.snippet: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts Humanitarian conditions...
world.content:
Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.

The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.

“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.

The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”

The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.

“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”

Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.

Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.

Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.

A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.

The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.

Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”

Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.

Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”

So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.

With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.

Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.

“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”

Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”

Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

world.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
world.snippet: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours Austrian police are hunting...
world.content:
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.

The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”

Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.

MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.

Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.

The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.

A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.

European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.

In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.

This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.

A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.
